fatal_errors: The predicted effect is reversed: aging-induced nanoprecipitates impaired or delayed formation of the protective Cr-rich scale and increased oxidation mass gain rather than producing more protective scales.
The relevant baseline is the nanoprecipitate-free, as-printed SLM alloy, not cast or wrought material.
The proposed in situ TEM oxidation conditions and 800–1050°C range are invented and omit the actual bulk isothermal comparison over 600–1200°C for up to 96 h.
No evidence supports the claimed improvement in oxidation resistance relative to cast or wrought counterparts; the reported 300–400 MPa advantage concerns strength, not oxidation resistance.
explanation: In situ environmental TEM with EDS could, in principle, visualize nanoscale redistribution and is a potentially useful supplementary method. However, it does not reconstruct the study, which compared as-printed and 750°C/50 h aged SLM material using bulk oxidation kinetics, cross-sectional SEM-EDS, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, and initial-state diffraction/microscopy. Most importantly, the hypothesis gives the wrong mechanistic direction: Cr-depleted L12/L21 precipitate regions and added matrix–precipitate interfaces delayed formation of a continuous protective Cr2O3 layer and supplied possible short-circuit oxygen paths. The aged alloy therefore gained more mass, especially at higher temperature, although both states ultimately benefited from Cr2O3 protection and had similar activation energies. Thin-foil TEM could also alter diffusion lengths, surface-to-volume ratio, oxide geometry, and gas exposure, so it cannot by itself establish representative bulk oxidation behavior.
